subject: maths

moments.title: Cardano and the cubic
moments.body:
Cardano publishes 'Ars Magna' containing a method to solve cubic equations. He had pried it from Niccolò Tartaglia under oath of secrecy and then published it anyway, citing earlier (and less complete) work by Scipione del Ferro.

Applied to certain cubics, the method requires taking square roots of negative numbers — even when the eventual answer is a real number. Cardano works with these but calls them 'sophistic' and 'mental tortures'.
moments.takeaway: Square roots of negative numbers force themselves into mathematics. They are useful, but no one quite trusts them.

moments.title: Bombelli works out the rules
moments.body:
Bombelli notices that combining 'sophistic' quantities by Cardano's rules can produce real numbers. He works out arithmetic rules for them: addition, multiplication, and (crucially) that 'piu di meno' (plus of minus) and 'meno di meno' (minus of minus) combine sensibly.

He applies the rules to specific cubics and gets correct real solutions. Imaginary numbers WORK as intermediate steps, even when the final answer is real.
moments.takeaway: The imaginaries gain operational rules. Their nature is still mysterious.

moments.title: Descartes coins 'imaginary'
moments.body:
Descartes uses the term 'imaginary' in his La Géométrie to describe roots of polynomials that don't correspond to real lengths. He intends it as a perjorative — these aren't real numbers, just useful fictions.

The name sticks. For two more centuries, mathematicians use imaginaries reluctantly.
moments.takeaway: An unflattering label that mathematics never escapes.

moments.title: Wessel, Argand, Gauss — the complex plane
moments.who: Caspar Wessel (Norway), Jean-Robert Argand (Geneva), Carl Friedrich Gauss
moments.body:
Wessel (Danish-Norwegian surveyor) and Argand (French bookseller-mathematician) independently propose representing complex numbers geometrically: as points in a plane, with the real axis horizontal and imaginary axis vertical. Multiplication corresponds to rotation and scaling.

Gauss writes the same picture in 1796 but doesn't publish until 1832. With his backing, the geometric interpretation becomes standard. The complex numbers are no longer ghostly — they form a 2D plane with concrete geometry.
moments.takeaway: Complex numbers become spatial. Geometry rescues them from the suspicion of unreality.

moments.title: Complex analysis flourishes
moments.body:
Cauchy develops residue theory, contour integration and complex analysis. Riemann introduces Riemann surfaces. Complex functions reveal structure that real analysis cannot see — for instance, the prime number theorem is most cleanly proved using complex analysis.

Quantum mechanics (1925-1926) makes complex numbers essential to physics: the wavefunction is intrinsically complex.
moments.takeaway: Complex numbers turn out to be FUNDAMENTAL to mathematics and physics, not mere intermediate fictions.

now.title: Complex numbers today
now.body:
Complex numbers are essential in physics (quantum mechanics, electrical engineering, signal processing), pure mathematics (number theory, geometry), and applied disciplines (control theory, fluid dynamics).

The Mandelbrot set and Julia sets live in the complex plane. Riemann's zeta function and the Riemann hypothesis are complex-analytic problems. Quaternions (a 4D extension by Hamilton, 1843) generalise complex numbers and are used in 3D graphics and aerospace.
now.open_questions: Why does quantum mechanics require complex numbers? (Recent experimental tests suggest it really does — real-valued quantum mechanics is empirically distinguishable.) Are there richer number systems that we will need in the future (octonions, Clifford algebras)? Why are some constants 'in love with' complex analysis (e to the i pi equals minus 1)?

reflection: Cardano's 'sophistic quantities', Descartes's 'imaginary numbers' — the names betray suspicion. It took 300 years for complex numbers to be accepted as mathematical objects on par with reals. Now they're indispensable. How does mathematics decide what's 'real'? And what does it tell us that the universe seems to insist on using complex numbers in its most fundamental equations?
